« On me dit : “Heureusement que je ne su: “‘I’m told, “Thank goodness I didn’t come”’ – Thousands of immigration candidates turn away from Quebec
Le durcissement de l’immigration au Québ: Quebec’s tightening of immigration rules is diverting thousands of Francophone candidates to other Canadian provinces.
Yacine Kraimia, analyste d’affaires et s: Yacine Kraimia, business analyst and recognized specialist in immigration policy. Photo credit: La Converse montage
Cet article repose sur une entrevue réal: This article is based on an interview with Yacine Kraimia, a business analyst and recognized specialist in immigration policy. It offers a rich and informed perspective on a moment of intense strain for thousands of international students and temporary foreign workers. The interview sheds light, on one hand, on the provincial government’s current choices and, on the other, on the worries and strategies of a group that is turning en masse, and desperately, to experienced voices to adapt to a shifting system.
Pour comprendre le contexte plus large d: To understand the broader context of the recent changes in immigration policy, I also consulted public data from the federal government and from Quebec’s ministère de l’Immigration, de la Francisation et de l’Intégration (MIFI), including Express Entry draws and selections under the Programme de sélection des travailleurs qualifiés (PSTQ). These facts were verified separately.
<strong>Depuis le durcissement des règle: Since Quebec tightened its immigration rules, culminating in the abolition of the Programme de l’expérience québécoise (PEQ) on November 19, immigration policy analyst Yacine Kraimia has been observing an unprecedented shift. The expert says that thousands of Francophone candidates hoping to immigrate to Quebec are heading instead to Ontario, New Brunswick and Alberta. “Right now, coming to Quebec is suicide,” he says.
À 19 h 45, après une journée qu’il décri: At 7:45 p.m., after a day he describes as “long and exhausting,” Yacine Kraimia still takes the time to speak with La Converse. In a calm voice, he describes his volunteer work this way: “I try to give information, to guide, to point people in the right direction.”
Informaticien de formation, il est deven: A computer scientist by training, he became a business analyst and has also made a name for himself through his ability to break down the laws, programs and political cycles that shape immigration in Canada and Quebec.
Sa page Facebook rassemble aujourd’hui p: His Facebook page now has more than 800,000 followers, a success he attributes to his expertise, his ability to anticipate immigration policies and his knack for simplifying the most complex measures: “I can tell when laws are coming. I inform people. In a way, I prepare them for the shock.”
Pour lui, la politique canadienne et qué: In his view, Canadian and Quebec immigration policy follows regular cycles: periods of openness, then of closure. “Every four or five years, the cycle repeats. When the economy is doing well, they want immigrants. When there’s a crisis, they close the door.” He adds that every 10 to 15 years, a major crisis hits, citing the slowdown in migration that followed the 2008 economic crisis and the post-Covid period.
Dès que la conversation glisse vers la s: As soon as the conversation turns to the situation in Quebec, his face lights up and his voice grows louder, almost cutting. The <l1>abolition of the PEQ, announced by the Quebec government on November 19</l1>, is only part of the equation, says Yacine Kraimia.
« Attention, on parle plus du PEQ parce: “Careful, we’re talking more about the PEQ because it’s the biggest of the programs. But there are also the three pilot programs that expire in January,” he explains. These are the pilot program for food processing workers, the pilot program for orderlies, and the pilot program to attract skilled workers in artificial intelligence, information technology and visual effects. “All of that disappears,” Kraimia warns.
Il décrit une transformation profonde du: He describes a profound transformation of Quebec’s immigration model. The PEQ, widely used by students and temporary workers, operated without a cap: “You meet the conditions, you get your CSQ (Quebec Acceptance Certificate, editor’s note). It was clear.” With the new PSTQ (the Special Skilled Workers Program is the new Quebec program replacing the PRTQ and the PEQ, editor’s note), the logic changes completely: “With the PSTQ, what they’re saying is, ‘Submit your applications and we’ll see who we select.’ And there’s a limited number. They’re going to select 1,000 people a month, when foreign workers and students number in the hundreds of thousands.”
Au fil de la conversation, Yacine Kraimi: Throughout the conversation, Yacine Kraimia keeps returning to the messages he receives. “People are frustrated, they’re desperate. I feel for them. People are crying. They tell me, ‘I sold everything in my country, I got my experience, my kids are in school, and now I know I won’t be accepted.’”
Ceux qui vivent à Montréal ou à Laval se: Those living in Montréal or Laval feel particularly trapped, he says. “The minister said it: in Montréal and Laval, they won’t be accepted. What do you expect them to do? They’ve been working here for three years, their kids are in school. They have no options,” Kraimia adds.
Selon lui, les critères d’acceptation da: According to him, the acceptance criteria under the PSTQ are complex: “They look at, for example, where you got your experience, where you’ll work, whether you have a job offer, which city it’s in, where you live, where you’re going to live… It’s complicated, and the conditions are very granular.”
Jusqu’ici, le Québec demeurait la destin: Until now, Quebec remained the preferred destination for Francophones wanting to immigrate to Canada, particularly those from the Maghreb countries, sub-Saharan Africa and France.
À la suite des récents changements, le v: Following the recent changes, the tide seems to be turning, observes Yacine Kraimia. “Before, I got thousands of messages a day from people interested in coming to Quebec. Now they tell me, ‘Thank goodness I didn’t come, I’m going to change my mind,’” he reports.
Il évoque une tendance « massive » : « P: He speaks of a “massive” trend: “Nobody wants to come to Quebec right now. We’re talking about thousands of people turning away. The French? Forget it. Algerians, Moroccans too.” Indeed, since the provincial government imposed an eight-month moratorium on the PEQ and the PRTQ – starting October 31, 2024 – the federal government, for its part, has opened the door to Francophone candidates for the rest of Canada.
Ottawa avait augmenté à ce moment-là de: At that time, Ottawa raised from 6% to 10% the share of permanent residences granted to Francophone immigrants choosing to settle outside Quebec. “I put very aggressive targets in my immigration plan, [namely] going up to 10% in Francophone communities outside Quebec. I would even be ready to welcome these people because they are brilliant people,” said Marc Miller, Canada’s immigration minister, on October 31, 2024.
Les chiffres des derniers tirages réalis: The figures from the latest draws under Express Entry (which groups the programs for granting permanent residence in Canada, outside Quebec) in the “French language proficiency” category are telling: 10,500 candidates invited for the two draws held in October 2025 alone.
Pendant ce temps, depuis le lancement du: Meanwhile, since the PSTQ was launched last July, and despite the Quebec immigration ministry’s promises to hold a draw every two weeks, there have been only a few<l1> rounds held in July and August</l1>, and only about a thousand candidates have been selected, all of them living outside Greater Montréal.
<strong>« Déposez au PSTQ, mais préparez: “Apply to the PSTQ, but prepare a plan B”
Maintenant que le Québec a aboli le PEQ: Now that Quebec has abolished the PEQ and tightened its selection criteria under the PSTQ, Francophone candidates are turning to other provinces. Among the followers of Yacine Kraimia’s Facebook page, two provinces stand out in particular: Ontario (especially Ottawa) and New Brunswick, both already popular in recent years. “Ottawa is Francophone and Anglophone, close to Montréal. People like that.”
Le Nouveau-Brunswick, dit-il, attire en: New Brunswick, he says, is attractive because of the simplicity of its programs: “With a college diploma and 18 months of study, you can apply for permanent residence. It’s simpler than here.”
Les provinces de l’Alberta et de la Sask: Alberta and Saskatchewan are also mentioned, even though English is a challenge for Francophones. On the other hand, he says, people from the Maghreb already know about New Brunswick’s programs, and this option, once marginal, has become central.
Sur d’autres réseaux sociaux consacrés a: On other social media groups devoted to advice on immigrating to Canada, the mood is just as grim. On the VF Immigration Facebook page, for example, a user affected by the abolition of the PEQ calls the PSTQ Hunger Games, a reference to the film featuring deadly trials.
S’adressant aux candidats à la résidence: Addressing permanent residence candidates living in Quebec, Kraimia proposes a two-step strategy: “If you meet the criteria, apply to the PSTQ. But don’t wait too long.” He recommends preparing a plan B right away: “Look at the other provinces. An expression of interest isn’t a commitment. Apply elsewhere too.”
Pour les personnes qui sont encore à l’é: For those still abroad, his advice is blunter: “Don’t come to Quebec. Right now, it’s suicide. The PSTQ is a lottery. A million people play, one or two win. There’s no guarantee.”
Les manifestants montrent leurs pancarte: Protesters show their signs to passersby and the media present. Photo credit: Charline Caro
Face à la mobilisation des résidents tem: Given the mobilization of temporary residents following the abolition of the PEQ, is there a chance the Quebec government will change its mind?
Interrogé à ce sujet, l’expert n’exclut: Asked about this, the expert does not rule out a possible reversal by the Legault government, “provided the pressure is fierce.” He also recalls a precedent: “In 2019, they wanted to tighten the conditions for accessing the PEQ. There were two months of fierce protests. The government ended up backing down and implemented a grandfather clause.”
Selon lui, la rapidité de la réaction du:
In his view, the speed of the immigration minister’s and the premier’s reaction to the <l1>protest held on November 17 in front of the MIFI headquarters in Montréal</l1> can only be the result of pressure from the street. “Usually, this minister doesn’t talk to anyone, doesn’t listen to anyone, he’s stubborn. […] This time, he reacted quickly in a television interview, and right afterward we saw the premier react too, saying, ‘There will be no grandfather clause.’ What does that mean?”

According to Yacine Kraimia, these rules won’t last: the political cycle will change and the CAQ should leave power in October. But he warns that the Parti québécois, the projected favourite, could extend or strengthen the restrictions. An improvement is therefore not certain in the short term. “It could get worse before it gets better,” the immigration expert concludes.
Il estime que les conséquences économiqu: He believes the economic consequences will force a change of course: “In education alone, international students bring a lot of money to Quebec (<l1>$4.2 billion in 2022</l1>, editor’s note). If you cut their numbers to a quarter, some schools will close.” An unthinkable prospect, he believes, that will lead the next government to loosen some immigration provisions.
